overview: This record maps the late Dutch East Indies, a vast colonial state governed from Batavia and inhabited by many peoples with different languages, religions, family systems and local authorities. The years 1920 to 1938 belong to the atlas record, not to the colony’s full lifespan: its 1938 outline is silently reassigned to another Dutch id and colonial rule continued until Japan’s 1942 conquest. During these years schools, medicine, engineering, astronomy, archaeology, cities and nationalist organizations expanded, but access and power were deeply unequal. Children built new ways to learn, workers and families survived plantations and depression, and activists imagined Indonesia. The outline is a broad locator. It cannot prove uniform Dutch control, one culture, or one daily routine across thousands of islands.

periods.title: Higher learning, narrow political voice
periods.summary: A technical college opened in Bandung in 1920, while the Volksraad still offered only constrained representation under colonial authority.

periods.title: Taman Siswa and competing ideas of education
periods.summary: Taman Siswa offered a child-guiding, anti-coercive educational vision while the Ethical Policy’s schools and public works continued to serve colonial purposes as well as public needs.

periods.title: Constrained debate, revolt and Boven Digoel
periods.summary: Political debate remained constrained, then the state crushed communist-led uprisings in West Java and West Sumatra and interned many opponents far from home.

periods.title: PNI, the Youth Pledge and women’s organizing
periods.summary: The PNI demanded independence; young delegates declared one homeland, nation and unifying language; women’s organizations assembled across religious and political lines.

periods.title: Arrests and the Depression
periods.summary: Colonial authorities arrested PNI leaders as collapsing export earnings brought wage cuts, job losses and insecurity to Java’s towns.

periods.title: New PNI under an assembly ban
periods.summary: Activists kept organizing after the 1933 meeting ban by using small secret gatherings and underground networks; leaders including Hatta and Sjahrir were arrested in 1934.

periods.title: A moderate petition rejected
periods.summary: Soetardjo and allies requested a conference toward self-government within the kingdom. The Dutch government’s 1938 rejection damaged hopes for gradual reform.

periods.title: The atlas id ends; colonial rule does not
periods.summary: The same map shape continues under another atlas id after 1938. Dutch effective rule ended only with Japan’s 1942 conquest, four years after this record’s cutoff.

sections.title: How to read this many-island map

items.text: The exact atlas id appears only from 1920 to 1938. Its two snapshots use the same MultiPolygon: 15 separate outer rings and 908 coordinate positions. That tells us the importer reused a coarse outline for navigation. It does not tell us where authority was strong, negotiated or resisted on the ground.

In 1938 the identical archipelago outline continues with the label “Dutch East Indies” but the civ id changes to netherlands-1878. Nothing constitutional happened to the colony that year. This is a database handoff hiding in plain sight, so the card will not invent a 1938 fall.

The broad geometry reaches from northern Sumatra to western New Guinea and excludes Portuguese Timor around Dili. Yet coastal point tests can miss cities because the coast is simplified, and fifteen rings cannot inventory thousands of islands. Think “where to look,” not “perfect border tracing.”

“Dutch East Indies” names a colonial state, not one civilization. Javanese, Sundanese, Minangkabau, Acehnese, Balinese, Chinese Indonesian, Indo-European, Papuan, Moluccan and many other communities lived within or across its claimed boundaries. A fact about one town or people is labelled that way below.

A governor-general and colonial administration held decisive power. The Volksraad, opened in 1918, contained appointed as well as elected members and began with advisory authority. Indonesians could debate and petition there, but it was never an equal parliament chosen freely by the whole population.

Colonial law sorted people into Europeans, the Indigenous population and “Foreign Orientals,” each connected to different bureaucracies, courts, procedures and taxes. Real lives did not fit tidy boxes, but paperwork could make a legal category shape schooling, work, travel, property and punishment.

The 1920 income tax was announced as one progressive scheme for residents aged fifteen and older above an income threshold. Actual taxation still varied by place and depended on local officials, village leaders and negotiation. A rule printed in Batavia was not automatically a uniform experience on every island.

After the 1926 to 1927 revolts, the government sent political prisoners to Boven Digoel in New Guinea. The remote camp isolated them from families and political networks under surveillance. Newspapers helped make the place a warning, while censorship shaped what readers could know.

The PNI, founded in 1927, sought Indonesian independence without cooperation with colonial rule. Authorities prosecuted and exiled leading nationalists. Repression could reach family life too: arrest or distant exile removed a wage earner, parent, child or sibling as well as a political organizer.

When public meetings were banned in 1933, New PNI members met secretly in small groups and reorganized underground. Cadre education helped the movement survive, even as police monitored, searched and arrested leaders. A “classroom” for politics might now be someone’s crowded front room with everyone listening for footsteps.

The 1936 Soetardjo petition asked for a conference to plan greater self-government within the Dutch kingdom, not immediate separation. The government waited until 1938 and rejected it. That refusal frustrated moderate nationalists who had tried the colony’s own official channel.

There was no single “Indies family.” Households and social life differed sharply by community, religion, place and wealth. Colonial legal status added another layer: officials tried to rank people by racial categories even when ancestry and daily cooperation did not fit their filing boxes.

A surviving Minangkabau example shows why local detail matters. At Nagari Sijunjung, descent and inherited property follow women’s lines, married couples are matrilocal, and a rumah gadang can house an extended clan. Male maternal relatives and elected penghulu also hold defined leadership roles.

The same Sijunjung record places houses beside rice fields, plantations, markets, mosques, a madrasah, graves and a customary hall. Children could learn clan knowledge in the rumah gadang as well as religion in a school. This is an enduring Minangkabau setting, not a model for Java, Bali or New Guinea.

The First Indonesian Women’s Congress met in Yogyakarta in December 1928. Seven groups initiated it, thirty organizations attended, and the official heritage account estimates about 700 participants. They did not all share one program, but coordination itself made women visible as national political actors.

Photographs record moments, not average lives. A 1925 album shows a front gallery, dining room and carpets in a Tjimahi home belonging to a Dutch family. It is useful evidence for one comparatively comfortable European household, and terrible evidence for what most Indigenous families owned.

By the 1930s, fewer than one quarter of Indigenous children were enrolled in primary school. Villages often carried much of the cost, while government spending favored schools for children with European legal status and ethnic Chinese children. Many children learned through family, religion, apprenticeship and work instead.

Bandung’s technical college opened in 1920 with one faculty and one major: road and water engineering. Its first class had 28 students, only two of them Indonesian. Four Indonesian students were among those who graduated as engineers in 1926. Higher education grew, but the doorway stayed very narrow.

Taman Siswa, founded in 1922, offered a different idea of school. Its Among system rejected forcing children and described the teacher as a pamong, a guide who supports development. It also argued that education should not belong only to society’s upper layers.

School and work often overlapped. Colonial policymakers debated limits on women’s and children’s labor, but employers defended cheap labor and described work as “natural” for Indonesians. The problem was not that children never learned; it was that the state invested little in giving most of them a real choice.

Youth organizations from Java, Sumatra, Sulawesi, Batak and Betawi communities joined student groups at the 1928 congress. Their resolution named a shared Indonesian homeland, nation and language. A tiny, privileged school population could still produce ideas that travelled far beyond campus gates.

Most daily work never appeared in a famous speech. Census categories recorded agriculture, food and textile production, retail and domestic service, while much subsistence and communal farm work went uncounted. The mix changed by place, gender and class; there was no responsible “average Indonesian job.”

The 1930 census of Java and Madura registered an occupation for nearly 30 percent of married women, especially in farming, food or textile production and retail. Yet it excluded much subsistence and communal agricultural work. The official number was large, and still managed to miss work.

On Sumatran tobacco and rubber estates, many workers had been recruited from China and Java. Contracts backed by penal sanctions restricted movement, and desertion remained common. Oil palm was becoming an estate crop by the 1930s. “Modern plantation” could mean modern export profits and very old-fashioned coercion.

The worldwide Depression devastated export-crop earnings. In Java’s towns, some workers endured wage cuts and worse conditions; others lost jobs, took casual work or returned to their home villages, where relatives supported them. A family network could function like unemployment insurance, without forms, offices or enough money.

Colonial “development” mixed help with extraction. Ethical Policy irrigation could aid rice cultivation, but it also served sugar production; schooling supplied clerks and workers; resettlement policy also aimed to prevent protest. An impressive canal or classroom does not answer the crucial question: who chose it and who benefited?

sections.title: Meals, clothes, homes and a little fun

items.text: A Java stereograph dated broadly 1900 to 1935 shows a warung with food displayed on a table. That is evidence of a small prepared-food business, not a menu: the catalogue cannot tell us whether the day’s star dish was rice, noodles, vegetables, sweets or something else. History sometimes leaves us hungry for labels.

Different islands, communities, religions and household budgets did not produce one colonial menu. The catalogue does not identify even the foods on this table, and the photograph belongs to inland Java. It cannot responsibly stand in for the entire archipelago, or even every Javanese dinner.

A cotton shoulder cloth from central Java shows indigo-and-white geometric batik. Historically, some patterns signaled rank, and court “forbidden patterns” were once restricted to nobility, though rules loosened. Clothes could keep sun off your shoulders and quietly announce where you stood in society, multitasking fabric!

The neat Tjimahi dining room and the Minangkabau rumah gadang are both real homes, yet they differ in community, household form, status and purpose. Placing them side by side shows why neither can serve as an all-purpose “Indies house.” Materials and floor plans followed local needs and resources.

Photographs were usually taken by people who could afford cameras, and catalogues often preserve the collector better than the cook, vendor, carpenter or child in view. Whenever a picture looks effortlessly “typical,” ask who pointed the lens, who supplied the caption and who never got named.

People sought help from family knowledge, midwives, herbal specialists, religious healers, Indigenous physicians, pharmacies, clinics and hospitals. These systems overlapped. Colonial medical-school records illuminate trained doctors especially well, so silence about another healer must never be mistaken for proof that the healer did not exist.

STOVIA in Batavia and NIAS in Surabaya trained Indies physicians. The civil service became the Public Health Service in 1925, and a university-equivalent Batavia Medical School opened in 1927 beside a hospital and laboratory. These were major institutions, but they produced only a small number of highly qualified doctors.

Some students received bursaries for books, food and other expenses, then owed ten years of relatively low-paid colonial medical service. Indonesian physicians treated patients and built careers while facing lower status and discrimination from European colleagues. A white coat did not erase the colony’s color line.

In the 1920s, malaria teams developed “species sanitation”: identify the breeding habitat of the local Anopheles mosquito species, then change that habitat. It was clever ecology, not one magic swamp-draining recipe. A historical review says it worked only in a few local situations with the right technical and social conditions.

Mosquito control, clinics and medical schools were achievements; access remained uneven by race, class, employer and location. A plantation laboratory or Batavia teaching hospital could not make a doctor appear on a distant island. “The colony had modern medicine” and “this child could reach it” are different claims.

sections.title: Water, washing and the all-important toilet question

items.text: Batavia’s water network was spectacularly unequal. In 1929, 6,926 kampong households received a combined 24 litres per second while 10,392 European households received 84. The chapter calculates that Europeans were about 7 percent of residents yet consumed 78 percent of residential piped water.

Many kampong residents collected water from public hydrants or vendors rather than a tap at home. Free network water was curtailed by a 1926 paid-delivery rule, and demand dropped sharply. Pipes existed, but price and connection rules determined whether clean water actually reached a cooking pot.

Colonial reformers often described kampongs as lacking pipes, drains, washing places and water closets. Their reports reveal real infrastructure gaps and also their prejudice: some writers blamed residents and used contemptuous language while protecting an unequal city. The source must be read for plumbing and power at the same time.

Toilets were not one archipelago-wide technology. The urban chapter records planners complaining about missing water closets and sanitation, but it cannot tell us what share of families used a private, shared or non-piped facility. Evidence is strongest for city projects, weakest for a trustworthy “typical toilet.” No honest historian can flush that uncertainty away.

Water history includes household use and the work of collecting it, not just pipes. Official plans count infrastructure more easily than the time and sore arms needed to bring vendor or hydrant water home. A network map therefore captures only part of daily labor.

sections.title: Science, preservation, music and written voices

items.text: Bosscha Observatory was inaugurated in 1923 after an astronomy society formed in Bandung and donors funded instruments. It became a lasting research and teaching institution and passed to the Indonesian government in 1951. The telescope outlived the colonial state, and kept looking much farther than any empire ever reached.

The colonial Archaeological Service began full restoration at Candi Panataran in 1918. Director Bosch brought Javanese dignitaries onto an advisory committee and shared results with students and teachers; the Depression then stopped most reconstruction. Calling this “discovery” would erase the communities who already knew the monuments.

At Ngandong in the early 1930s, Geological Survey work uncovered ancient human braincases in a Solo River bone bed. A 1932 report used the name Homo soloensis; later researchers classify the finds as Homo erectus and have revised their age. Discovery is a process: the fossils stayed still while scientific labels moved around them.

Authentic 1928 writing sample: “KAMI POETRA DAN POETRI INDONESIA” means “WE, THE SONS AND DAUGHTERS OF INDONESIA.” It uses period Malay/Indonesian spelling in Latin letters. It is one line from a political resolution, not a sample of Javanese, Balinese or the archipelago’s many other written languages.

The same decision pledged one homeland, one nation and a unifying language, Bahasa Indonesia. That was a political choice made by youth organizations amid enormous linguistic diversity. A shared public language could connect islands without making home languages disappear.

At the Second Youth Congress, journalist-musician W. R. Soepratman played Indonesia Raya without lyrics to reduce the danger of colonial repression. Imagine a room hearing a future national anthem while authorities still ruled the country it imagined. Sometimes a violin can make a very political noise.

ending.text: The exact map id stops in 1938 because its unchanged geometry is reassigned, not because the Dutch East Indies ended. Japanese forces conquered the colony in 1942. Sukarno and Hatta proclaimed Indonesian independence on 17 August 1945; the Netherlands refused and fought to restore control before transferring sovereignty on 27 December 1949. Western New Guinea initially remained under Dutch administration and disputed. Dutch colonial government ended through conquest, revolution, war and negotiation; peoples, families, languages and local histories continued.
